metadata.title: Real Art, New Light: Museums and artists are finding ways to use AI to bring people closer to actual artworks, with the original staying exactly where it belongs: at the center.
metadata.topic: ART & AI — AI THAT SENDS PEOPLE BACK TO THE REAL THING
metadata.register: Warm, simple, friendly -- short sentences, no jargon; thoughtful and fair, with respect for the artworks, and clear about what is illustration and what is reported, per the user's explicit tone request.
metadata.note: Sourced from the user-supplied article 'Real Art, New Light' (pasted directly in the build request; references: Kemp 2021 (The Jakarta Post, an AFP wire report on the Rijksmuseum's Night Watch edges), Sarmiento 2019 (Palm Beach ArtsPaper, the Dali Museum), Chan 2023 (Wallpaper*) and Alemdar n.d. (TRT World, no visible date) on Refik Anadol's Unsupervised at MoMA, Levine 2026 (The Boston Globe) and Kenny 2026 (HBR Cold Call) on Harvard Art Museums, and Ludwig Museum Koblenz 2026 -- see FACTCHECK.md). User asked for a 'Deep Explainer' at exactly 4:00. The toolkit's actual deep-explainer skill targets 5-10 min and requires ~20-25% of body beats to be pantry/archival stills sourced through a two-gate pipeline. Both conflict with this request: a hard 4:00 target, and the user's own note that no footage exists and that no real artwork or likeness may be shown. Built instead on the ai-explainer chassis (Claude composer cold open -> presenter intro -> body -> sources note -> handoff -> outro), reusing the all-self-generated Manim/Remotion approach and af_bella/@HumanitariansAI branding used on this user's other reels. The host self-introduction ('Hi, I'm Agrima') lives in its own B00B presenter-intro beat. COVERAGE (per the user's explicit instruction): Rembrandt/Rijksmuseum, the Dali Museum and MoMA are covered in full (about 25 seconds each); Harvard Art Museums and Ludwig Museum Koblenz get one sentence each in a single beat (B06). The 'three habits' (B02) and 'ideas anyone could borrow' (B07) are kept short. HEDGING: the Rijksmuseum story is said, in narration and on screen, to come from a wire report; the Dali review is said to be from 2019 and the controversy about bringing back a deceased artist is stated fairly; the opening scene (B01) and the borrowable ideas (B07) are labeled illustrations and the author's own suggestions, not reported cases. NO REAL ARTWORKS OR LIKENESSES (user instruction): the painting, the Night Watch frame and the portraits are generic abstract shapes, the Dali figure is a faceless generic silhouette, visitors are plain figures; NO museum or company logos (all names are plain text); every visual is a generated Manim graphic. The user's explicit tone request (warm, simple, friendly; thoughtful and fair) is a deliberate departure from this chassis's default Teardown register -- disclosed here.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW -- ask shown answered; no self-intro here (see B00B)
beats.narration_text: I asked Claude to help me picture a moment: standing in front of a real painting, with a little help.

props.command:
claude "what could AI add to a visit
  without touching the painting?"
output: the painting stays exactly as it is
a screen shows the brushwork up close
you look at the real thing differently

beats.role_note: presenter intro -- 'Hi, I'm Agrima' + lead-in; doubles as the EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY beat
beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Agrima. Today: how museums and artists use AI to bring people closer to real art.
beats.visual_intent: presenter card: name, then a short lead-in

beats.role_note: illustration: a painting seen only on postcards, a screen with the brushwork up close, a guide that answers questions; the painting has not changed; the question is what we ask AI to do -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: You're standing in front of a painting you've only seen on postcards. Beside it, a screen shows the brushwork up close, and a guide answers your questions. The painting hasn't changed. But you're looking at it differently. This is an illustration, not a real case. The question isn't whether AI belongs in museums. It's what we ask it to do. Help people notice the real thing, and interesting projects appear.
beats.visual_intent: illustration: a gallery wall with a generic illustrated painting, a small screen beside it showing brushstrokes up close, a guide speech bubble and a plain visitor figure; labeled 'illustration -- not a real case'; ends on 'what we ask it to do'

beats.role_note: three habits that keep the art authentic: original untouched and the star; AI built from the art's own materials; visitors told what is AI and what is real -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Three habits keep the art authentic. One: the original stays untouched, and stays the star. Two: the AI is built from the art's own materials, like the artist's words, scans, or the museum's collection. Three: visitors are told what is AI, and what is real.
beats.visual_intent: a three-item numbered checklist, each row ticking on as it is said: original stays untouched and stays the star; AI built from the art's own materials (the artist's words, scans, the museum's collection); visitors are told what is AI and what is real

beats.role_note: 1715: cut down on all four sides, strips never found; Rijksmuseum used AI to imagine the edges, a smaller 17th-century copy as guide, three neural networks matched to Rembrandt's style; printed on canvas and mounted on frames around the painting for three months (restoration project launched 2019); original not repainted; from a wire report (Kemp, 2021) -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Example one: Rembrandt's The Night Watch. In 1715, it was cut down on all four sides to fit a wall in Amsterdam's town hall, and the strips were never found. The Rijksmuseum used AI to imagine the missing edges, with a smaller seventeenth-century copy as a guide and three neural networks trained to match Rembrandt's style. The new sections were printed on canvas and mounted around the painting for three months. The original was not repainted. This comes from a wire report.
beats.visual_intent: a generic abstract painting frame with four dashed extension strips and a '3 months' label; chips for 1715 cut on four sides, a smaller 17th-century copy as guide, three neural networks, printed on canvas and mounted around it, original not repainted; a 'wire report' source chip; no real artwork depicted

beats.role_note: Dali Museum, Florida: a life-size AI Dali greets visitors on screens; script from his own writings, quotes, interviews and archival footage, performed by an actor; offers a selfie at the end; a reviewer called it complementary to a strong permanent collection; seen as controversial by some; the review is from 2019 (Sarmiento, 2019) -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Example two: the Dalí Museum in Florida. A life-size AI version of Salvador Dalí greets visitors on screens. The script is built from his own writings, quotes, interviews, and archival footage, performed by an actor. At the end, he offers to take a selfie. A reviewer called it complementary to a strong permanent collection. Some saw bringing back a deceased artist as controversial. And that review is from 2019.
beats.visual_intent: a faceless generic silhouette on a screen with a speech bubble (no likeness of any real person); chips for his own writings, quotes, interviews, archival footage / performed by an actor / a selfie at the end; a 'complementary to a strong permanent collection' note; 'seen as controversial by some' and 'review from 2019' tags

beats.role_note: MoMA: Refik Anadol's Unsupervised filled a 24 ft x 24 ft lobby wall with imagery generated from 320,000 visual inputs from the collection; sensors picked up light, movement and weather; a team of 15; a collaboration between people and machines; first generative AI artwork MoMA acquired; the real artworks were the raw material (Chan, 2023; Alemdar, n.d.) -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Example three: MoMA. Refik Anadol's Unsupervised filled a twenty-four by twenty-four foot lobby wall with moving imagery, generated from three hundred and twenty thousand visual inputs from the museum's collection. Sensors picked up light, visitors' movement, and the weather, and a team of fifteen shaped the results. Anadol calls it a collaboration between people and machines. It became the first generative AI artwork MoMA acquired. The real artworks were the raw material.
beats.visual_intent: a large square wall of flowing abstract colour with three stat cards: 24 x 24 ft, 320,000 inputs, team of 15; chips for sensors (light, movement, weather) and 'first generative AI artwork MoMA acquired'; 'the real artworks were the raw material'

beats.role_note: one sentence each: Harvard Art Museums sent a talking version of an 18th-century portrait to its mailing list, no original touched, an invitation back to the painting, openly AI (Levine, 2026; Kenny, 2026); Ludwig Museum Koblenz continued a real exhibition online as a walkable digital twin with an AI guide art professionals can train (Ludwig Museum Koblenz, 2026) -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Two more, briefly. Harvard Art Museums sent a talking portrait to its mailing list, with no original touched, after its marketing director talked with curators first. He called it an invitation back to the painting. Ludwig Museum Koblenz continued a real exhibition online as a walkable digital twin, with an AI guide its own art professionals can train.
beats.visual_intent: two small panels: an inbox/envelope with a framed portrait silhouette (Harvard), and a walkable room with a guide icon (Koblenz), each with a one-line caption

beats.role_note: the author's own suggestions, not rules: let the artist do the talking; put anything AI-made beside the real artwork and say which is which; keep it temporary; end with an invitation to see the real thing; show your workings; talk to your experts first -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Ideas anyone could borrow. These are my own suggestions, not rules. Let the artist do the talking. Put anything AI-made beside the real artwork, and say which is which. Keep it temporary, so the AI is a guest. End with an invitation to see the real thing. Show your workings, like Anadol sharing his data sources. And talk to your experts first.
beats.visual_intent: a six-item list labeled 'my ideas, not rules', each row appearing on its sentence: let the artist do the talking; put AI-made things beside the real work and say which is which; keep it temporary; end with an invitation to see the real thing; show your workings; talk to your experts first

beats.role_note: closing idea: edges re-seen, an artist speaking from his own words, a collection as moving light; art has always met new tools; replace the original or send people back to it; these projects chose the second; that choice keeps the work authentic -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: A painting re-seen with its missing edges. An artist speaking from his own words. A collection turned into moving light on a wall. Art has always met new tools, from the camera to the projector. The choice each time is to use the tool to replace the original, or to send people back to it. These projects chose the second. That choice, more than the technology, keeps the work authentic.
beats.visual_intent: a visitor (plain figure) looking at a real frame; three captions (edges re-seen, his own words, moving light); then the choice: replace the original / send people back to it, with the second highlighted

beats.role_note: the Rijksmuseum story comes from a wire report; the Dali review is from 2019; the opening scene and the ideas anyone could borrow are illustrations and suggestions, not reported cases -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: A note on sources. The Rijksmuseum story comes from a wire report. The Dalí review is from 2019. The TRT World article shows no date. And the opening scene and the ideas anyone could borrow are illustrations and suggestions, not reported cases.
beats.visual_intent: a sources card (plain-text references, no logos) with on-screen notes: wire report (Rijksmuseum), 2019 review (Dali), illustrations and suggestions (opening scene, borrowable ideas)
